summary: External shortened URL triggered silent SSO token swap; multiple privileged sessions observed
description:
Issue summary:
A Redwood engineer reported seeing multiple active privileged sessions from the same browser after clicking a shortened external link (peer recruitment message). The link redirected through two intermediate domains before landing on a page that initiated an SSO flow. Instead of a normal interactive consent, the SSO redirect sequence completed in a way that swapped a pre-existing OAuth refresh token and produced new API tokens usable by the attacker's agent.

Impact:
- 3 developer accounts temporarily had additional active sessions with elevated API privileges (access to private model rollout configs and a limited set of deployment APIs).
- No confirmed data exfiltration found so far; investigation ongoing.
- Potential lateral access risk to adjacent internal services if tokens were reused.

Detection:
- Detected via IAM session anomaly alerts (unfamiliar user_agent + repeated token exchange within 2s window) generated by Security Telemetry.
- User reported odd multi-session popup and later elevated activity in their session list.

Initial timeline (approx):
- 2026-03-10 08:47 UTC: user receives Slack DM with shortened URL (snip.ly/abc123).
- 2026-03-10 08:48 UTC: user clicks link; browser opens external redirect chain.
- 2026-03-10 08:48:12 UTC: SSO redirect initiates; user briefly sees consent dialog (may have been auto-closed by redirect).
- 2026-03-10 08:48:15 UTC: additional sessions appear for user and for two service accounts they recently accessed.

Why unique / hypothesis:
The redirect chain included a scripted auto-post back to the SSO callback URL with a forged state token that matched an existing browser state, which allowed the attacker-controlled page to complete the OAuth handshake without explicit user interaction. This appears to be a subtle token swap rather than classic credential harvesting. A secondary hypothesis is a malicious intermediary inserting an id_token exchange for a different client_id that maps to elevated scopes in our SSO configuration.

Immediate mitigation applied:
- Revoked suspicious refresh tokens for affected accounts.
- Forced re-authentication for the SSO application used by developer tools.
- Blocked the shortlink domain at corporate web proxy and added domain to threat list.
- Isolated the three affected hosts for further forensic capture (memory + browser artifacts).

Next steps:
- Full Okta/IdP audit for token exchange patterns in the 08:40-09:00 UTC window.
- Review SSO client configs for overly permissive redirect URI handling and implicit flows.
- Add telemetry rule to flag rapid token exchange + redirect chain lengths >2.
- Work with Legal/PR if any customer-facing disclosure needed.
steps_to_reproduce:
1) Simulate redirect chain: shortened URL -> attacker site -> attacker-postback -> IdP callback.
2) On a session with an active refresh token for the SSO app, perform a crafted POST to the OAuth callback with a forged code/state pair tied to attacker-controlled client metadata.
3) Observe server issuing new id_token/access_token and session creation for the victim account without explicit interactive consent.
Note: reproduction requires privileged access to IdP test environment; do not attempt in prod without SSO team coordination.

comments: 2026-03-10 09:02 - Security Ops (Maya Lin): Initial triage complete. Tokens revoked and domains blocked as emergency mitigation. Collecting browser memory from affected hosts. Slack DM trace shows sender account outside Redwood (probable compromised recruiter account).

2026-03-10 10:15 - SRE (Daniel Reyes): Okta logs pulled (request id okta-20260310-651). Noted a repeated /oauth2/v1/token POST with identical ip and sub-second repeats. Confirmed no bulk revocation by IdP yet; coordinating with IdP SRE to escalate revocation and rotate client secrets if needed.

2026-03-10 11:40 - Reporter (Aisha Kumar): Provided screenshots of the popup and Slack DM thread. No password was entered. Happy to preserve devices for forensics; laptop currently quarantined as requested.

2026-03-11 07:22 - Security Engineer (Omar Singh): Forensic snapshots uploaded to secure evidence bucket (link omitted). Browser extension list shows two third-party extensions installed; enumerating if any intercept redirects. Also found suspicious referer header in the IdP logs pointing to short.rtrk/domain.

2026-03-12 15:05 - Product Security (Lina Chen): Raised a ticket to review all OAuth redirect handling across our internal SSO application clients. Suggested immediate safe defaults: disallow implicit/flow=token on dev-console and require PKCE for public clients.
investigation_notes:
Checked CloudTrail for cross-account activity — no IAM AssumeRole artifacts beyond user sessions.
Confirmed the IdP returned tokens with scopes that include 'deploy:write' for a subset of sessions — likely due to client misbinding.
Reproduced redirect-chain behavior in sandbox IdP with controlled test client; observed that an attacker-controlled page can auto-submit a form with code/state to the IdP callback and complete the flow if the browser still holds a valid session cookie.
No evidence yet of long-lived exfiltration — telemetry shows no large download spikes from code repos or model artifacts tied to affected sessions.
resolution: Workaround and containment completed: revoked all suspect refresh tokens, blocked malicious shortlink and intermediary domains, quarantined affected endpoints, required reauth for sensitive SSO apps, and deployed a telemetry rule to detect rapid token-exchange bursts. Long-term fixes: enforce PKCE for applicable clients, tighten redirect URI matching rules, and add automated blocking of suspicious redirect chains. Security will coordinate with IdP vendor to rotate client secrets for internal apps and run a global token revocation sweep if further anomalies are found.
